html:
A war of about 261 BCE in which the Maurya emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga, an independent kingdom on the east coast of India, in today's Odisha. Its bloodshed is said to have turned Ashoka toward Buddhism.

Kalinga controlled the coast and the land routes between north and south India, which made it a prize. Ashoka attacked in about the eighth year of his reign. The battle is traditionally placed near the Dhauli hills by the Daya river, close to modern Bhubaneswar.

Almost all we know comes from Ashoka himself. In his thirteenth rock edict he says that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 were killed, and many times that number died. He writes that he felt remorse for the suffering of ordinary people, and that conquest by dhamma, moral teaching, was now the only conquest he valued. It is a rare thing: a conqueror publicly regretting his own war. At Dhauli itself the edicts carved on the rock leave out that confession and instead tell officials to treat the people justly.

This was Ashoka's only major war and it closed the age of Maurya expansion. Some historians point out that he was already a lay Buddhist before it, and that later Buddhist writers dramatised his conversion.

Kalinga regained its independence after the Mauryas. In the 1st century BCE its king Kharavela made it a strong power of its own.
sum: A war of about 261 BCE in which the Maurya emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga, an independent kingdom on the east coast of India, in today's Odisha. Its bloodshed is said to have turned Ashoka toward Buddhism.
